findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. Within seconds they can say what the site is about and why it matters.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why it is mostly about a different project (firstmate): the study is a demonstration of Athena. A newcomer can follow that, but the title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" names a project they have probably never heard of.
findings.source: Header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The next step is concrete and close at hand: a link at the top jumps to prerequisites, a clone command, ./setup.sh and a one-line example. A newcomer knows exactly what to do next.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page never shows what Athena's own output looks like, such as a traced commit, a cost record or a verdict. The newcomer has to take the main selling points on trust.
findings.source: Header lede: "records what each step cost" / "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: This link sits in the header with no explanation. A first-time visitor does not know whose proposals these are or whether the link is meant for them.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is dense detail about firstmate internals: exit codes, pending-close records, places-held. Someone evaluating Athena will likely skim or give up here. It works as proof of rigor, not as an introduction.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Claims and sources"

findings.text: Terms are defined twice, and many entries say "The firstmate source does not define…". This is honest, but it makes the page longer and more hedged than a newcomer needs.
findings.source: Glossary vs. "Words used first": entries for "in scope", "red", "green", "yolo" repeated nearly word for word

findings.text: Each claim carries a "mechanism" or "prose-only" tag, but the page never explains either one. A reader checking claims has to guess what they mean.
findings.source: Claims list tags "mechanism" and "prose-only"; Glossary defines "mark" but not these tags

findings.text: The page has no section or card called "concurrency entry". This reference points at nothing a reader can find.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f2: "The page attaches those claims to the counter, to the relaunch transition, to the queued state and to the concurrency entry."

findings.text: This section uses internal repository detail without saying which repository holds the studies/ folder. It means little to a newcomer.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
